newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria rebel group says will fight on.
newsitem.headline: Algeria rebel group says will fight on.

text.p: With more than 70 people slaughtered in two days of massacres in Algeria, a Moslem militant group which claims not to target civilians has vowed to pursue the conflict against Algeria's authorities.

In a faxed statement on Tuesday, the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS) -- the armed wing of Algeria's outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) -- denied reports that large numbers of rebels were surrendering. It said the reports were part of a media campaign to "mutilate the image of jihad (holy struggle) in Algeria".
It was not possible to authenticate the statement, which was faxed to an international news agency in Paris.
Both the AIS and the FIS have distanced themselves from the indiscriminate killing of civilians, blamed by most Algerian commentators mainly on the Armed Islamic Group (GIA).

The statement, dated July 26, added: "This campaign also aims at deluding people that large numbers of 'gunmen' have surrendered to the forces of tyrants as a prelude to the total collapse of the 'armed groups'...(and aimed) at spreading the spirit of defeat in the hearts of the warriors and their supporters."
The statement made no reference to a large-scale operation by the security forces earlier this month in which up to 300 rebels died, according to Algerian newspapers.
News reports said these rebels were GIA members. Nor did it mention massacres in which suspected rebels killed hundreds of civilians in recent weeks.
Rebels armed with knives and guns killed more than 70 people in attacks earlier this week, apparently revenge for the military offensive carried out in the past two weeks.
There was no official confirmation of the orgy of bloodshed in which the influential daily El Watan said a one-year-old baby was beheaded and a pregnant woman disembowelled.
But most Algerian newspapers reported the massacres on their front page -- seen as a sign that the authorities acknowledged the killings and had given the green light for them to be reported.
About 60,000 people have now died in the conflict which started shortly after the authorities cancelled a general election in which the FIS had a huge lead.
The first massacre this week was carried out by about 100 rebels who stormed Si Zerrouk hamlet near Larba area shortly after midnight on Sunday and burst into homes, Liberte newspaper said.
"They broke open the houses and then cut the throats of the residents, sparing none, neither men nor women and even babies," the newspaper said.
Most newspapers put the massacre toll at 47 dead while Le Matin newspaper said 58 villagers might have perished.
Rebels the same night slaughtered 22 villagers in Aonaria hamlet in Medea province, 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers, slashing their throats or gunning them down, El Watan said.

The killings brought the toll among villagers in the past week to more than 170 in Blida and Medea provinces. Hundreds have died in massacres in the past two years that the authorities blame on Moslem rebels.

Earlier this month, FIS chief Abassi Madani was freed from jail, half way through a 12-year term for threatening state security. He vowed shortly after his early release from jail that he and his supporters would strive to stop the bloodshed.
